blocks.content: Path based routing split one hostname many ways. Host based routing does the opposite: it splits many hostnames across the exact same single entry point. Between the two, every real Ingress rule you will ever write is fully accounted for.
Host Based Routing, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: Host Based Routing, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: Host based routing is the Ingress mechanism that directs a request to a specific backend Service based on the hostname the request is targeting, specified through the standard HTTP Host header sent with every request.

A request for api.example.com and a request for app.example.com can both arrive at the exact same Ingress controller, at the exact same external IP address, and still be routed to two entirely separate backend Services based purely on that hostname.

This is expressed in an Ingress manifest through the host field at the top of each rule, distinct from the path based paths array covered in the previous topic, though the two are frequently combined within the very same rule.

Host based routing is the mechanism that allows dozens, or even hundreds, of genuinely distinct public domains to share one single load balancer and one single Ingress controller, which is often the single largest source of the cost savings promised throughout this module.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643071929-439057025.png
blocks.alt: Host based routing given its own full depth

blocks.content: Many Domains, One Shared Address

In DNS terms, every domain routed through the same Ingress controller points, through an A record or a CNAME record, at the exact same external IP address or hostname, the one belonging to the controller's own front facing load balancer.

The Ingress controller, upon receiving a request, reads its Host header and consults its own internal routing table, built directly from every Ingress object's host rules, to determine which backend Service that specific domain should be forwarded to.

This means adding an entirely new public facing application to a cluster often requires no new cloud infrastructure at all, just a new DNS record pointing at the existing address, plus one new host rule added to an Ingress object.

This is a genuinely significant operational simplification compared to the one load balancer per application pattern warned against in the previous module, collapsing what could be dozens of separate external addresses down to just one.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643073507-50783366.png
blocks.alt: A domain name determining which Service receives the request

blocks.content: A Real Host Based Routing Example
blocks.text: A Real Host Based Routing Example

blocks.content: Returning to the same company introduced in the very first topic of this module, running a marketing site, an API, and an admin dashboard, host based routing is precisely the mechanism that earlier example's three separate host rules relied on.

api.example.com, app.example.com, and admin.example.com each resolve in public DNS to the exact same load balancer address, and the Ingress controller's host based rules are what correctly separates traffic for each domain to its own distinct backend Service.

A new fourth domain, say docs.example.com for a documentation site, requires only a new DNS record and one new host rule appended to the existing Ingress object, with zero changes required to any of the three already running applications.

This example demonstrates concretely and completely why host based routing, more than any other single mechanism covered in this module, is what makes Ingress genuinely scale gracefully as an organization's number of public facing applications grows over time.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: company-ingress
spec:
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-service
                port:
                  number: 80
    - host: app.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: frontend-service
                port:
                  number: 80

blocks.content: Recap: The Other Half of the Routing Vocabulary
blocks.text: Recap: The Other Half of the Routing Vocabulary

blocks.content: The previous topic covered path based routing in full, splitting one hostname across many paths, each directed to a distinct backend Service, entirely within a single shared domain name.

Host based routing is the direct complement to that mechanism, splitting traffic across many hostnames instead, and together the two cover essentially the complete range of routing decisions any real Ingress manifest ever needs to express.

Neither mechanism is inherently superior to the other. The right choice between them, or the decision to combine both together, depends entirely on how an organization's specific applications are naturally structured and branded externally.

Having now covered both halves of this vocabulary in full, dedicated depth, the next section of this topic shows exactly how the two combine within a single Ingress object, which is genuinely the most common real world pattern of all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643076716-301754551.png
blocks.alt: Recap of path based routing as the other half of the vocabulary

blocks.content: Combining Host and Path Rules Together
blocks.text: Combining Host and Path Rules Together

blocks.content: A single Ingress object can, and very often does, combine host based rules with path based rules nested inside them, letting a single domain serve multiple applications while multiple domains simultaneously share the same controller.

For example, api.example.com might itself be split further by path, with slash v1 routing to a legacy API Service and slash v2 routing to a newer API Service, all nested underneath that one host rule within the exact same Ingress object.

This combined pattern is genuinely the most powerful and most common real world configuration, since it gives an organization full, fine grained control over both which domain and which path any given request is routed by, entirely through one declarative manifest.

Mastering this combination, rather than treating host based and path based routing as separate, unrelated tools, is what separates a basic understanding of Ingress from genuine, production ready fluency with it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643078367-867960151.png
blocks.alt: A single Ingress combining both host and path rules together

blocks.content: A Common Mistake: Forgetting to Update DNS
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: Forgetting to Update DNS

blocks.content: A very common mistake, precisely because it lies outside Kubernetes itself, is writing a perfectly correct host based Ingress rule and then forgetting to actually point that domain's real DNS record at the Ingress controller's external address.

The Ingress rule can be entirely correct, and the controller can be entirely healthy, but if the domain's DNS record still points at an old address, or does not exist at all, no real user traffic will ever actually reach the new rule.

This mistake is diagnosed quickly by checking DNS resolution directly, using a tool such as dig or nslookup against the domain in question, and confirming it resolves to the exact same address the Ingress controller's own Service is currently using.

This is a genuinely important reminder that Ingress, however powerful, only controls routing after a request has already arrived at the cluster. Getting that request there in the first place remains entirely the responsibility of DNS, configured separately.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784643080006-956551719.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of forgetting to point DNS at the Ingress controller address

blocks.content: Wildcard Host Rules

Some Ingress controller implementations support wildcard host rules, such as star dot example dot com, matching any subdomain of example.com that is not otherwise matched by a more specific host rule elsewhere in the manifest.

This is genuinely useful for platforms that dynamically create a new subdomain per customer or per environment, letting a single wildcard rule handle every current and future subdomain without requiring a new Ingress rule for each one individually.

Wildcard support and its exact matching behavior differ between Ingress controller implementations, making this a case where checking the specific controller's own documentation is genuinely necessary rather than assuming universal, consistent behavior.
For most applications with a small, well known, fixed set of domains, explicit host rules remain the clearer, more predictable, and more commonly recommended choice over a wildcard rule.
Host Based Routing and Multi Tenant Platforms
blocks.text: Host Based Routing and Multi Tenant Platforms

blocks.content: Host based routing is the foundational mechanism behind many multi tenant software as a service platforms, where each customer receives their own subdomain, such as customer-name.platform.com, all routed through the exact same underlying Ingress controller and cluster.

This pattern lets a platform scale to thousands of distinct customer facing domains without provisioning any new infrastructure per customer, since the routing decision is made entirely by the Ingress controller reading each request's Host header.

Combined with the wildcard host rule capability just covered, this pattern can be implemented with a genuinely small number of Ingress rules, even as the actual number of served customer domains grows into the thousands over time.
Recognizing this pattern is useful both for building this kind of platform and for correctly understanding the architecture of many real world SaaS products already running on Kubernetes today.
Host Based Routing and Certificate Scope
blocks.text: Host Based Routing and Certificate Scope

blocks.content: Every distinct host routed through Ingress that needs to serve HTTPS traffic requires its own certificate coverage, either through an individual certificate for that exact hostname or through a wildcard certificate covering it as one of many subdomains.

This connects directly to the TLS topic immediately following this one, where certificate management is given its own full, dedicated depth, but it is worth flagging here since host based routing is precisely what determines how many distinct hostnames actually need that coverage.

Planning host naming conventions with certificate scope in mind, for example consistently using subdomains of a single parent domain rather than scattered, unrelated domains, can meaningfully simplify certificate management later, as covered fully in the next topic.

This is a small but genuinely useful piece of forward planning: decisions made here about how domains are structured directly shape how much certificate management complexity the very next topic's practices need to account for.
Host Based Routing With Subdomains vs Separate Domains
blocks.text: Host Based Routing With Subdomains vs Separate Domains

blocks.content: Organizing applications under subdomains of one parent domain, such as api.example.com and app.example.com, versus using entirely separate, unrelated domains for each application is a genuine architectural decision worth making deliberately rather than by accident.

Subdomains of one parent domain simplify DNS management, since a single wildcard DNS record can often cover every current and future subdomain, and they simplify certificate management through the wildcard certificate pattern covered in the previous section.

Entirely separate, unrelated domains offer stronger brand separation and can be genuinely necessary when different applications are marketed to different audiences under entirely distinct product names, at the cost of more individual DNS and certificate management overhead.
Neither approach is universally correct, and the right choice depends heavily on branding and organizational requirements that go beyond what Kubernetes or Ingress configuration alone can determine.
A Real World Host Based Routing Failure Mode
blocks.text: A Real World Host Based Routing Failure Mode

blocks.content: A subtle but real failure mode occurs when a host rule is added to an Ingress manifest and applied successfully, but the corresponding DNS record change has not yet propagated fully across every DNS resolver a real user's request might pass through.

During this propagation window, some users reach the newly configured application successfully while others, served by a resolver that has not yet picked up the change, still receive the old behavior or no resolution at all, producing confusing, inconsistent bug reports.

Understanding DNS propagation delay as a genuinely real, time bound phenomenon, rather than assuming a DNS change takes effect instantly and universally everywhere, prevents unnecessary panic and misdirected debugging effort during this specific window.

Waiting a reasonable propagation window, typically well under an hour for most DNS providers, before concluding a host based routing change has genuinely failed is a small but valuable piece of operational patience worth building into any deployment runbook.

blocks.title: Operational Note
blocks.content: DNS changes are not instantaneous everywhere. Inconsistent reports immediately after a host rule change are often a propagation delay, not a routing bug.
Host Header Validation and Security

Because host based routing relies entirely on the HTTP Host header, and that header is technically supplied by the client making the request, a well configured Ingress controller validates it strictly against known, configured host rules rather than trusting it blindly.

This validation prevents a class of attack where a malicious client sends a request with a forged or unexpected Host header attempting to reach a backend Service that was never intended to be exposed under that specific hostname.

Most mainstream Ingress controller implementations handle this validation correctly and safely by default, but it is worth understanding as one more reason relying on well maintained, widely used controller software, rather than a custom built alternative, is generally the safer choice.

This security consideration closes the loop on host based routing as a genuinely complete topic: not just how it works, but why it can be trusted to work correctly and safely even against deliberately malformed or malicious incoming requests.
Best Practices for Host Based Routing
blocks.text: Best Practices for Host Based Routing

blocks.content: Keep a single, authoritative source of truth for which domains map to which backend Services, whether that is the Ingress manifests themselves or a separate internal documentation page kept rigorously in sync with them.
Verify DNS resolution explicitly as a standard step after adding or changing any host rule, rather than assuming a DNS record was correctly created or updated elsewhere as part of the same change.

Combine host and path rules deliberately within a single Ingress object when an application genuinely needs both, rather than creating unnecessary, harder to maintain separate Ingress objects for what is really one logical routing configuration.

Document any wildcard host rule clearly, including exactly which specific host rules take priority over it, since wildcard matching behavior is one of the less immediately intuitive aspects of Ingress configuration for engineers new to it.

blocks.content: The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

Host based routing completes the routing vocabulary this module has been building since its first topic, letting many entirely distinct public domains share one single load balancer, one single Ingress controller, and one single cluster entry point.

Combined with path based routing from the previous topic, it gives an Ingress manifest full, expressive control over exactly how any incoming request, regardless of its domain or its path, should be routed to the correct backend Service.
The next topic, TLS, covers how these same host rules are secured with HTTPS, extending the exact same per domain granularity already established here to certificate management as well.

Keep the DNS plus Ingress rule pairing firmly in mind. A correct Ingress rule with no matching DNS record, or a correct DNS record with no matching Ingress rule, both result in the exact same frustrating, unreachable outcome.

One final, practical reminder before moving on: DNS propagation takes real, if usually brief, time, and confusing early symptoms during that window are far more often a timing issue than a genuine configuration mistake.

With both path and host based routing now fully covered, the next topic layers HTTPS security directly on top of every host rule established here, completing the routing and security picture together.
Host based routing is now fully covered; TLS, securing every domain established through it, follows immediately next.
Every domain routed through this topic's examples now has a clear, deliberate destination, and the next topic ensures every one of them can be reached securely.

blocks.title: Host Based Routing In Full
points: Host based routing directs requests to different backend Services based on the HTTP Host header, letting many domains share one single Ingress controller and one single external address.
It is the direct complement to path based routing, and the two are frequently combined within a single Ingress object for full, fine grained control.
A correct Ingress rule has no effect until the domain's DNS record actually points at the Ingress controller's external address, a distinct, easily forgotten step outside Kubernetes itself.
Wildcard host rules, supported by many but not all controller implementations, are genuinely useful for multi tenant platforms serving many dynamically created subdomains.
TLS, covered next, extends this same per domain granularity to HTTPS certificate management for every host rule established in this topic.
